extracted.intended_audience: general readers; people interested in 19th-century plantation life and practical plantation procedures
extracted.subtask_description: A first-person narrative describing practical methods and social practices on Southern plantations: how to construct a fish-trap, how cane is planted/hoed/cut, the sugar-house manufacturing process, holiday customs, and the role/qualifications of overseers and drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fish-trap construction (frame and movable bottom)
rubrics_metrics.description: A frame between two and three feet square is made, and of a greater or less height, according to the depth of water. Boards or slats are nailed on three sides of this frame... A door is fitted into the fourth side, in such manner that it will slide easily up and down in the grooves cut in the two posts. A movable bottom is then so fitted that it can be raised to the top of the frame without difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an auger hole in the centre of the movable bottom with a loosely turning handle that ascends to the top of the frame; fit many gimlet holes in the handle and insert small sticks extending to opposite sides so a fish cannot pass without hitting one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fish-trap triggering and baiting
rubrics_metrics.description: The trap is 'set' by sliding up the door and kept there by a stick resting in notches on the inner side and in the handle; bait it by rolling a handful of wet meal and cotton until hard and deposit in the back part of the frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a fish swims toward the bait it strikes a small stick, turning the handle, which displaces the supporting stick; the door then falls and secures the fish. Draw up the movable bottom to the surface by the handle to retrieve the catch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing ground and drills for planting sugar cane
rubrics_metrics.description: The ground is prepared in beds, the same as for cotton seed, but ploughed deeper. Drills are made similarly. Planting commences in January and continues until April.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant a sugar field only once in three years; three crops are taken before the seed or plant is exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cane planting arrangement and spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Three gangs employed: one draws the cane from the rick cutting top/flags; another lays the cane in the drill, placing two stalks side by side so that joints will occur once in four or six inches; the third gang hoes, drawing earth upon the stalks and covering them to the depth of three inches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure tops and green portion are removed (green juice sours molasses). After about four weeks sprouts appear and grow rapidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hoeing and crop schedule for cane
rubrics_metrics.description: A sugar field is hoed three times, the same as cotton, with a greater quantity of earth drawn to the roots. By the first of August hoeing is usually over. In the middle of September, whatever is required for seed is cut and stacked in ricks. In October it is ready for the mill and the general cutting begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-year cane is sweeter and yields more than the first; the third year yields more than the second; after three crops the field must be ploughed and replanted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winrowing to prevent frost and souring
rubrics_metrics.description: If a planter apprehends a frost, the cane is winrowed: cutting the stalks early and throwing them lengthwise in the water furrow so the tops cover the butts. They will remain three weeks or a month without souring and secure from frost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proper time arrives, take up, trim and cart to the sugar-house.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing field for succeeding crops (burning refuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: In January the ground is strewn with tops and flags from the last year's cane; on a dry day fire is set to this combustible refuse which sweeps over the field, leaving it bare and clean and ready for the hoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loosen the earth about the roots of the old stubble; in time another crop springs from last year's seed until exhaustion after third year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cane-knife specification and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: The blade of a cane-knife is fifteen inches long, three inches wide in the middle, and tapering towards the point and handle. The blade is thin, and in order to be at all serviceable must be kept very sharp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every third hand takes the lead of two others; lead hand shears flags, cuts the top down to green, severs stalk at root, and lays it behind him; companions place their stalks upon his.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of cutting gangs and cart system
rubrics_metrics.description: Every third hand leads two others; to every three hands there is a cart which follows; younger slaves throw stalks into the cart which is drawn to the sugar-house and ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead hand must carefully separate green from ripe parts (green sours molasses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sugar-house (mill) processing sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Cane is unloaded onto an endless carrier conveying it into the main building where it falls between two great iron rollers and is crushed; juice falls into a conductor into a reservoir, then through five filterers (filled with bone-black) in succession, into a large reservoir, pumped into clarifiers heated by steam, passed through successive clarifiers into close iron pans with steam tubes, then to coolers with sieve bottoms so syrup grains and molasses escapes into a cistern below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bone-black (calcinated bones) in filterers to decolorize. Coolers are wooden boxes with finest wire sieve bottoms; when syrup meets air it grains into white/loaf sugar, which is then packed in hogsheads for market. Molasses is processed separately into brown sugar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of cane refuse in mill
rubrics_metrics.description: After crushing, the cane falls upon another carrier that conveys it out of the main building depositing it in the top of a chimney upon a fire beneath which consumes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burning refuse prevents the building from filling and prevents souring and disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holiday allowance and customary length
rubrics_metrics.description: The only respite from constant labor the slave has through the whole year is during the Christmas holidays. Epps allowed three—others allow four, five and six days, according to the measure of their generosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holidays are the time of feasting, frolicking, and fiddling—the carnival season for the enslaved; slaves may also be given passes or paid to remain and labor during remaining holidays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs and dress for Christmas supper and festivities
rubrics_metrics.description: Slaves array themselves in best attire; cotton coats washed, shoes improved with tallow, hats worn if available; women wear handkerchiefs or red ribbons—red is the favorite color. Table spread in the open air with varieties of meat and vegetables; seating males on one side and females on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooking may be in kitchens or by burying meat over coals; white people often assemble to witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music, dance and patting as communal entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: After supper comes the Christmas dance; violin and banjo accompaniment; 'patting' (hand/leg percussion) and song used when fiddle stops. 'Patting' involves striking hands on knees, together, shoulders while keeping time with feet and singing simple songs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music provides consolation and social mobility for the narrator; dancing continues until broad daylight and may shift into patting and singing with unmeaning but rhythmic lyrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications and armament of overseers
rubrics_metrics.description: Overseers ride into the field on horseback, armed with pistols, bowie knife, whip, and accompanied by several dogs. The requisite qualifications in an overseer are utter heartlessness, brutality and cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their business is to produce large crops regardless of human suffering; pistols are for dangerous emergencies; dogs are to overhaul fugitives or those unable to keep up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and discipline of black drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Drivers are black, who in addition to performing equal share of work, are compelled to do the whipping of their several gangs. Whips hang around their necks, and if they fail to use them thoroughly, are whipped themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Driver numbers scale with field size; drivers enforce discipline under threat of punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slave marriage practice under plantation law/custom
rubrics_metrics.description: The only ceremony required is to obtain the consent of the respective owners. Either party can have as many husbands or wives as the owner will permit, and either is at liberty to discard the other at pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If spouses live apart, visits allowed on Saturday nights if distance permits; plantation owners may encourage marriage of female slaves.
